transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor... I suppose what brings me in is... well, it’s a heavy thing to admit out loud, isn't it? I’ve just been sitting in my chair by the window most days, watching the leaves fall, and I keep having this thought... this persistent, heavy thought that just settles right in my chest and won't leave. I look at my wife—she’s been so good to me all these years, truly an angel—and I think about the kids, they have their own lives now, their own families to worry about, and I just... I keep thinking they would all be so much better off if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow morning. It sounds terrible, I know, but it feels like a fact. Just a cold, hard fact. I’d be out of their way. And lately, I’ve even caught myself saying it out loud to her. Just the other day, I was looking out at the frost on the grass, and I told her, 'I really don’t need to see another winter.' I don't know why I said it, but I meant it. I just... I feel like I've seen enough winters, you know? And the cold just seems to be seeping into my bones lately, into my mind, and I just don't see the point in dragging them all through it with me anymore.
How long have you been feeling this way? Have these thoughts and feelings been present most days for at least two years, or did they start more recently?

Well, let me think... two years? No, no, it hasn't been that long. I can tell you exactly when the shift happened, actually. It was about a year and a month ago. You see, that was when my bowling partner, Arthur, passed away. We bowled together every Tuesday morning at the lanes down on 4th Street for... oh, it must have been fifteen years. We weren't just bowling partners, you know? We'd sit and have coffee afterward, talk about the world going to the dogs, talk about our knees aching... the usual things old men talk about. And then one Tuesday, he just didn't show up. Heart attack, right there in his kitchen. Ever since then, it’s just been... different. The world got quieter, but not in a peaceful way. More like a heavy, empty quiet. That’s when these thoughts really started taking root. I tried going back to the lanes a few times by myself, but looking at his empty chair... it just made the cold feeling worse. So, yes, it’s been about thirteen months now of this... this constant weight. Not two years, no, but long enough. More than long enough, if you ask me. It feels like an eternity some days, just sitting there, remembering how things used to be before Arthur went.
Have you noticed that you don’t take pleasure in things anymore—like bowling, or spending time with your wife, or other activities you used to enjoy?

Well... yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly it. It's not just the bowling, you see. It's... it's everything. I used to be quite the busybody, if I'm being honest. My wife and I, we used to play bridge every Thursday evening with the Millers. Have for years. We'd set out the good mixed nuts, make a pot of decaf, and play until nearly ten o'clock. I always looked forward to it, the strategy of it, the banter. But now... the thought of sitting at that card table, trying to remember who played what suit, making small talk about the weather... it just feels like climbing a mountain. I told her to go ahead and ask the Johnsons to take my place. I just can't bring myself to care who takes the trick anymore. 

And the garden... oh, I used to take such pride in my tomatoes. Big, beautiful beefsteaks. I'd be out there every morning at the crack of dawn, pulling weeds, checking for those awful little hornworms. I had a whole system with the stakes and the twine. This past spring, I didn't even buy the seedlings. The soil just sat there, turning to dust. My wife asked if I wanted her to pick some up at the nursery, but I just looked out the window at the empty plot and felt... nothing. Just a heavy nothing. 

Even the things I didn't have to work at, the things I just enjoyed... they're gone too. I used to love helping out with the cooking for the church potlucks. I made a baked ziti that people would ask for by name. I'd spend all afternoon Sunday simmering the sauce, getting the seasoning just right. The last time they had a potluck, I just sat in my chair. I couldn't even muster the energy to boil the water. And the Cubs... heavens, I've been a Cubs fan since I was a boy listening on the radio. I used to watch every game, keep score in a little notebook I kept by the remote. Now, the television just stays off. They could win the World Series again tomorrow, and I don't think it would make a lick of difference to me. I just sit in my chair by the window, like I said, and I look out, and I just... I can't make myself care about any of it anymore. The bridge, the tomatoes, the ziti, the baseball... it's all just noise now. Just exhausting noise.
Have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for at least the past two years?

Well, doctor, I know you asked about the two years just a moment ago, but... no, it hasn't been two years. I'm quite certain of that. Like I was saying about Arthur, it was just over a year ago. Thirteen months, to be precise. Before that, well, I was still myself, you know? I was still planting my tomatoes, still watching my Cubs, still bowling my Tuesday games. I had my routine. I liked my routine. I'd wake up at six-thirty, have my coffee—black, no sugar, the way I've taken it since I was in the service—read the paper from front to back, and then start my day. I wasn't sitting in this chair all day back then. I was out in the world, doing things, being a part of things. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I've felt this way for two years. It really did just start after Arthur passed. That was the turning point. It's like someone just flipped a switch, or maybe... maybe more like someone slowly turned down the volume on everything good, until all that was left was this heavy, quiet sadness. And it is every day now, yes. Most of the day, nearly every day. From the moment I wake up and look at the ceiling, I just feel this weight pressing down on my chest, telling me there's no point in getting up. But it's been thirteen months of this, not two years. Thirteen months of just... existing, really. Not living. Just existing in that chair by the window.
Have you experienced any periods of time when you felt a bit more like yourself, where the sadness lifted even a little, for a few days or more, during the past thirteen months?

Lifted? No... no, I can't say that it has. Not even a little bit, doctor. Not for a day, not even for an afternoon. My wife, bless her heart, she keeps hoping for that, you know. Just this past Easter, she thought maybe... well, she thought having the house full of family would finally do the trick. She went all out. Baked a big ham with the pineapple rings and the cloves stuck in it, exactly the way I used to like it, and she had all three of the grandkids over. 

They were running around the front yard in their little Sunday outfits, hunting for those plastic eggs... and she just kept looking over at me, waiting for me to smile or to get up and help them look behind the azalea bushes like I always did. I used to be the one who hid the special golden egg, you see. I'd fold up a crisp five-dollar bill, tuck it inside, and hide it somewhere really tricky, like up in the crook of the old oak tree out front. I'd spend half the morning giving them hints, getting a real kick out of it. 

But this year... I just sat in my chair by the window watching them. I saw them running around, I heard them laughing and shouting when they found one, but it was like... like I was watching it all happen on a television set with the sound turned down, or through a thick pane of glass. The sadness didn't lift at all. The smell of the ham didn't make me hungry, the kids didn't make me smile. It's just this constant, heavy blanket over absolutely everything. 

Summer came right after that, and the heat was just terrible this year, and then autumn rolled in... the leaves turned brown and fell right off that same oak tree, and I just watched it all happen from the exact same spot in the living room, feeling the exact same way. Every single day just bleeds into the next. So, no, to answer your question... there haven't been any good days. There haven't even been any half-good days. It's just been a long, unbroken line of thirteen months feeling like I'm slowly sinking right through the floorboards.
Have you felt a lack of energy or noticed that even small tasks feel exhausting most days?

Energy? Well... I'm not quite sure what you mean by that, doctor. Do you mean physical energy? Because if you're asking if my body is tired, then no, I haven't noticed that at all. I know I said earlier that things felt exhausting, but... I didn't mean my muscles were weak, or that I was out of breath or anything of that sort. My body is actually in very good shape for an eighty-year-old man. 

Dr. Henderson—he's my general practitioner over on Elm Street, I've been seeing him since the late nineties—he checked my heart and my blood pressure just a few months back. He hooked me up to all the machines, made me walk on that little treadmill they have in the back room. He told me, he said, "You have the constitution of a man ten years younger." I've always prided myself on my stamina, you see. Even just a couple of years ago, before Arthur passed, I used to walk down to Miller's Hardware every single Saturday morning. Two miles there, two miles back, and I never even broke a sweat. I could still do that walk today if I had a reason to. 

So if you're asking if taking out the trash or sorting the mail makes me physically exhausted, no, it doesn't. My wife, bless her, she gets confused by it. She'll ask me, "Are you too tired to help me dry the dishes tonight?" And I always tell her, "No, Martha, I'm not tired at all." My arms work perfectly fine. My legs work. I don't feel sleepy during the day. I just... I sit in my chair because there's absolutely no point in getting up, not because I lack the physical strength to do it. So I'm really not sure how to answer your question. If you mean am I physically fatigued by small chores, then no, I haven't noticed anything like that. I just don't do them.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight over the past thirteen months?

Appetite? Weight? Well, doctor, I suppose Martha might tell you differently if you asked her, but from where I sit, no, I haven't noticed any real changes there. None at all, really. I know she worries. She's a worrier, my Martha. Always has been. When we were first married, she used to worry if I was five minutes late getting home from the plant. 

But as for the food... well, I still eat exactly what I've always eaten. Like I was telling you earlier about my routine, I've always been a creature of habit when it comes to my meals. Breakfast is a bowl of oatmeal—plain, none of that sugary maple brown sugar nonsense in the little packets, just plain rolled oats—and a slice of wheat toast with a thin scrape of butter. Lunch is half a turkey sandwich on rye, maybe a small cup of whatever soup she's made, though usually it's just the sandwich. And dinner is whatever she puts in front of me. 

She still makes her pot roast on Sundays, she still does the meatloaf on Tuesdays, and she still insists on fish on Fridays, even though we haven't been to mass in a decade. I eat it all. I sit at the table, I pick up my fork, and I chew, and I swallow. I clean my plate just like I was taught to do when I was a boy growing up during the war, when you didn't dare leave a single pea behind because you didn't know when you'd see another one. 

So, no, my appetite hasn't changed. I'm not starving myself, if that's what you're getting at. Now, do I enjoy the food? Does the pot roast taste the way it used to? That's a different question entirely. Like I said about the Easter ham... it's just fuel now. It's just something I have to put in my mouth because Martha is watching me with those worried eyes of hers, and I don't want to hear her fret about it. But I'm eating the same amount. And my clothes... well, my trousers still fit exactly the same. I still buckle my belt on the third notch, same as I have since I retired in '05. The scale in the bathroom—the old mechanical one, not the digital kind that always breaks—it still hovers right around one hundred and sixty-five pounds, give or take a pound depending on the time of day. So no, doctor, no changes there. Just the same old routine, chewing and swallowing, day in and day out.
Have you felt like a burden to your family or experienced guilt over things you believe you've done wrong, or failed to do, since Arthur passed away?

Burden... guilt. Doctor, that's... that's really all there is now. That's the only thing that runs through my head when I'm sitting in that chair by the window. I just sit there, and my mind, it's like an old film reel that's gotten stuck, just playing the same terrible moments over and over again. I keep going over every little thing I did wrong with him... with Arthur. Every time I lost my temper when he was a boy, like that time in the summer of '78 when he left my good socket wrench out in the rain and it rusted, and I shouted at him until he cried. Why did I do that? It was just a piece of metal. And then when he got older, and I didn't call him as often as I should have, or when I didn't know what to say to him... I just keep replaying it all. Every failure. 

And not just with Arthur, but with my whole family. With Martha, too. I think about all the times I was late coming home from the plant when the boys were little, all the times she needed me to just listen and I was too busy hiding behind the evening paper. I look at her now, bustling around the kitchen, trying so hard to make me smile with her pot roasts and her grandkids, and I just feel this crushing weight because... well, because I know I'm just a weight on her now. I'm a terrible burden. I feel like I'm no good to anybody anymore. I just take up space in this house, dirtying a plate for her to wash, contributing absolutely nothing of value. I'm utterly useless to them. 

And to be perfectly honest with you, doctor... I know why this is happening to me. This whole thing, this... this heavy blanket and the sinking through the floorboards I told you about... I know it's my own fault. It's my penance. I failed them, you see. I was a poor father, a selfish husband, and I deserve whatever punishment is coming my way. I really do. I sit there in the living room every day just waiting for it to finally happen, because a man who has ruined things the way I have... well, he doesn't deserve peace. He deserves exactly what he gets. So yes, to answer your question, I go over it all, every single day, every single hour, just waiting for the gavel to fall.

patient.answer:
Appetite? Weight? Well, doctor, I suppose Martha might tell you differently if you asked her, but from where I sit, no, I haven't noticed any real changes there. None at all, really. I know she worries. She's a worrier, my Martha. Always has been. When we were first married, she used to worry if I was five minutes late getting home from the plant. 

But as for the food... well, I still eat exactly what I've always eaten. Like I was telling you earlier about my routine, I've always been a creature of habit when it comes to my meals. Breakfast is a bowl of oatmeal—plain, none of that sugary maple brown sugar nonsense in the little packets, just plain rolled oats—and a slice of wheat toast with a thin scrape of butter. Lunch is half a turkey sandwich on rye, maybe a small cup of whatever soup she's made, though usually it's just the sandwich. And dinner is whatever she puts in front of me. 

She still makes her pot roast on Sundays, she still does the meatloaf on Tuesdays, and she still insists on fish on Fridays, even though we haven't been to mass in a decade. I eat it all. I sit at the table, I pick up my fork, and I chew, and I swallow. I clean my plate just like I was taught to do when I was a boy growing up during the war, when you didn't dare leave a single pea behind because you didn't know when you'd see another one. 

So, no, my appetite hasn't changed. I'm not starving myself, if that's what you're getting at. Now, do I enjoy the food? Does the pot roast taste the way it used to? That's a different question entirely. Like I said about the Easter ham... it's just fuel now. It's just something I have to put in my mouth because Martha is watching me with those worried eyes of hers, and I don't want to hear her fret about it. But I'm eating the same amount. And my clothes... well, my trousers still fit exactly the same. I still buckle my belt on the third notch, same as I have since I retired in '05. The scale in the bathroom—the old mechanical one, not the digital kind that always breaks—it still hovers right around one hundred and sixty-five pounds, give or take a pound depending on the time of day. So no, doctor, no changes there. Just the same old routine, chewing and swallowing, day in and day out.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, which would support the diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F32.3) over persistent depressive disorder (F33.3).
doctor.question: Have you felt like a burden to your family or experienced guilt over things you believe you've done wrong, or failed to do, since Arthur passed away?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going over every little thing I did wrong with him and with my family, and I feel like I’m no good to anybody and deserve whatever punishment is coming.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of being a burden and experiencing guilt over past actions or failures, which directly corresponds to the symptom of worthlessness and guilt.

patient.answer:
Burden... guilt. Doctor, that's... that's really all there is now. That's the only thing that runs through my head when I'm sitting in that chair by the window. I just sit there, and my mind, it's like an old film reel that's gotten stuck, just playing the same terrible moments over and over again. I keep going over every little thing I did wrong with him... with Arthur. Every time I lost my temper when he was a boy, like that time in the summer of '78 when he left my good socket wrench out in the rain and it rusted, and I shouted at him until he cried. Why did I do that? It was just a piece of metal. And then when he got older, and I didn't call him as often as I should have, or when I didn't know what to say to him... I just keep replaying it all. Every failure. 

And not just with Arthur, but with my whole family. With Martha, too. I think about all the times I was late coming home from the plant when the boys were little, all the times she needed me to just listen and I was too busy hiding behind the evening paper. I look at her now, bustling around the kitchen, trying so hard to make me smile with her pot roasts and her grandkids, and I just feel this crushing weight because... well, because I know I'm just a weight on her now. I'm a terrible burden. I feel like I'm no good to anybody anymore. I just take up space in this house, dirtying a plate for her to wash, contributing absolutely nothing of value. I'm utterly useless to them. 

And to be perfectly honest with you, doctor... I know why this is happening to me. This whole thing, this... this heavy blanket and the sinking through the floorboards I told you about... I know it's my own fault. It's my penance. I failed them, you see. I was a poor father, a selfish husband, and I deserve whatever punishment is coming my way. I really do. I sit there in the living room every day just waiting for it to finally happen, because a man who has ruined things the way I have... well, he doesn't deserve peace. He deserves exactly what he gets. So yes, to answer your question, I go over it all, every single day, every single hour, just waiting for the gavel to fall.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a major depressive episode that has persisted for over one year following the death of a close friend, with persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, feelings of guilt, and suicidal ideation. The chronicity and duration of symptoms beyond 12 months, in the absence of manic or hypomanic episodes, supports the diagnosis of Recurrent Depressive Disorder, Current Episode Severe Without Psychotic Symptoms.
